result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_edges_str_repr()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get edges as formatted string representations. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L7187-L7317){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_edges_str_repr( limit=1000, use_labels=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Edges as strings](/assets/graphs/get-edges-str-repr.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph with node ids 1 to 4 in pills; the edge between B and C is outlined in the accent color. The table lists one string per edge, 'source--target', using node ids by default ('1--2' to '3--4') and labels with use_labels=True ('A--B' to 'C--D'); the B–C row, '2--3' and 'B--C', is highlighted." width="100%"} Returns one compact string per edge, showing its two endpoints joined by a connector that reflects the graph's directedness: - directed graphs: `"source->target"` - undirected graphs: `"source--target"` Strings are produced in edge insertion order, and parallel edges or self-loops each get their own entry (so the same string can appear more than once). This is a quick way to eyeball a graph's structure, for example: - printing or logging the edges of a small graph while building or debugging it - comparing two graphs' edge lists in a test (e.g. `sorted(...) == sorted(...)`) - producing readable edge listings for reports, using labels rather than numeric IDs For anything beyond display, prefer `get_edges_as_tuples()`, which returns the numeric `(edge_id, source, target)` triples without any string parsing. All edges in the graph are considered; the current node or edge selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [limit]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1000]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of edge strings to return, taken from the start of the insertion-ordered edge list. The default of `1000` keeps output manageable for large graphs. Pass `None` to return a string for every edge. A `limit=` of `0` returns an empty list. [use_labels]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), both endpoints are written as numeric node IDs. If `True`, each endpoint is written as its node label, falling back to the node ID (as a string) for any node that has no label. Label lookup happens per edge in Python, so `True` is slower than the default on large graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Edge strings such as `"1->2"` (directed) or `"A--B"` (undirected, with `use_labels=True`), in edge insertion order and truncated to at most `limit=` items. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} By default, edges are formatted using node IDs, with the arrow showing direction: ::: {#3f979d5c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.get_edges_str_repr() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['1->2', '2->3'] ``` ::: ::: Passing `use_labels=True` swaps in each node's label wherever one is available: ::: {#139a9e00 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A->B', 'B->C'] ``` ::: ::: Undirected graphs use a double dash instead of an arrow, since neither endpoint is the "source": ::: {#aac80883 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="X") .add_node(label="Y") .add_edge(source="X", target="Y") ) graph.get_edges_str_repr(), graph.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (['1--2'], ['X--Y']) ``` ::: ::: When a node has no label, `use_labels=True` falls back to its node ID. Here the third node is added without a label, so it shows up as `3` while the others use their names: ::: {#11533535 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="Alice") .add_node(label="Bob") .add_node() # no label; gets node ID 3 .add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob") .add_edge(source="Bob", target=3) ) graph.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['Alice->Bob', 'Bob->3'] ``` ::: ::: The `limit=` argument caps how many strings come back, counting from the first edge added; `limit=None` returns every edge: ::: {#b389f9ca .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_nodes([f"Node_{i}" for i in range(5)]) graph.add_edges([(f"Node_{i}", f"Node_{i+1}") for i in range(4)]) ( graph.get_edges_str_repr(limit=2, use_labels=True), len(graph.get_edges_str_repr(limit=None)), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (['Node_0->Node_1', 'Node_1->Node_2'], 4) ``` ::: :::
